claim: Drosophila Follicle Stem Cells (FSCs) are maintained by population asymmetry, where stochastic behaviors of multiple individual cells collectively result in a balance between stem cell division and differentiation.
source: Many adult stem cell communities are maintained by population asymmetry, where stochastic behaviors of multiple individual cells collectively result in a balance between stem cell division and differentiation. We investigated how this is achieved for Drosophila Follicle Stem Cells (FSCs) by spatially-restricted niche signals.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as the context for the study.

claim: FSCs produce transit-amplifying Follicle Cells (FCs) from their posterior face.
source: FSCs produce transit-amplifying Follicle Cells (FCs) from their posterior face and quiescent Escort Cells (ECs) to their anterior.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract describing FSC behavior.

claim: FSCs produce quiescent Escort Cells (ECs) to their anterior.
source: FSCs produce transit-amplifying Follicle Cells (FCs) from their posterior face and quiescent Escort Cells (ECs) to their anterior.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract describing FSC behavior.

claim: JAK-STAT pathway activity declines from posterior to anterior across the FSC domain.
source: JAK-STAT pathway activity, which declines from posterior to anterior, dictates the pattern of divisions over the FSC domain
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by reporter data shown in figures.

claim: JAK-STAT pathway activity dictates the pattern of divisions over the FSC domain.
source: JAK-STAT pathway activity, which declines from posterior to anterior, dictates the pattern of divisions over the FSC domain
evidence: This is a main finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: JAK-STAT pathway activity promotes more posterior FSC locations.
source: JAK-STAT pathway activity, which declines from posterior to anterior, dictates the pattern of divisions over the FSC domain, promotes more posterior FSC locations and conversion to FCs, while opposing EC production.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: JAK-STAT pathway activity promotes conversion of FSCs to FCs.
source: JAK-STAT pathway activity, which declines from posterior to anterior, dictates the pattern of divisions over the FSC domain, promotes more posterior FSC locations and conversion to FCs, while opposing EC production.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: JAK-STAT pathway activity opposes EC production.
source: JAK-STAT pathway activity, which declines from posterior to anterior, dictates the pattern of divisions over the FSC domain, promotes more posterior FSC locations and conversion to FCs, while opposing EC production.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: Wnt pathway activity declines from the anterior across the FSC domain.
source: Wnt pathway activity declines from the anterior, promotes anterior FSC locations and EC production, and opposes FC production.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by reporter data.

claim: Wnt pathway activity promotes anterior FSC locations.
source: Wnt pathway activity declines from the anterior, promotes anterior FSC locations and EC production, and opposes FC production.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: Wnt pathway activity promotes EC production.
source: Wnt pathway activity declines from the anterior, promotes anterior FSC locations and EC production, and opposes FC production.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: Wnt pathway activity opposes FC production.
source: Wnt pathway activity declines from the anterior, promotes anterior FSC locations and EC production, and opposes FC production.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: JAK-STAT and Wnt pathways combine to define a stem cell domain through concerted effects on FSC differentiation to ECs and FCs at either end of opposing signaling gradients.
source: The pathways combine to define a stem cell domain through concerted effects on FSC differentiation to ECs and FCs at either end of opposing signaling gradients, and impose a pattern of proliferation that matches derivative production.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main conclusion.

claim: JAK-STAT and Wnt pathways impose a pattern of proliferation that matches derivative production.
source: The pathways combine to define a stem cell domain through concerted effects on FSC differentiation to ECs and FCs at either end of opposing signaling gradients, and impose a pattern of proliferation that matches derivative production.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main conclusion.

claim: An egg chamber buds from the germarium every 12 hr under optimal conditions.
source: An egg chamber buds from the germarium of each of a female's thirty or more ovarioles (Figure 1A–D) every 12 hr under optimal conditions, requiring a high constitutive rate of FC production throughout adult life (Duhart et al., 2017; Margolis and Spradling, 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: FSCs were originally thought to be maintained by invariant single-cell asymmetry.
source: However, in the original study identifying FSCs an implicit assumption was made, in accord with contemporary precedents, that each FSC is long-lived and maintained by invariant single-cell asymmetry (Margolis and Spradling, 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: Individual FSCs are frequently lost or duplicated.
source: A comprehensive re-evaluation, which included the analysis of all FSC lineages, without any prior assumptions about their behavior, showed that individual FSCs were frequently lost or duplicated (Reilein et al., 2017)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: FSC differentiation to an FC is not temporally coupled to, or dependent upon division of the same FSC.
source: and that FSC differentiation to an FC was not temporally coupled to, or dependent upon division of the same FSC (Reilein et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: There are 14–16 FSCs arranged in three anterior-posterior (AP) rings anterior to the border of strong Fas3 protein expression.
source: Production of 5–6 'founder' FCs (the first FCs to associate with a germline cyst to seed the FC epithelium) per budding cycle is accomplished by 14–16 FSCs, arranged in three anterior-posterior (AP) rings anterior to the border of strong Fas3 protein expression, near the mid-point of the germarium (Figure 1A–D; Hayashi et al., 2020; Reilein et al., 2017; Reilein et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations and referenced to Figure 1.

claim: FSCs produce 5–6 'founder' FCs per budding cycle.
source: Production of 5–6 'founder' FCs (the first FCs to associate with a germline cyst to seed the FC epithelium) per budding cycle is accomplished by 14–16 FSCs, arranged in three anterior-posterior (AP) rings anterior to the border of strong Fas3 protein expression, near the mid-point of the germarium (Figure 1A–D; Hayashi et al., 2020; Reilein et al., 2017; Reilein et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: FCs derive directly from the posterior ('layer 1') FSCs.
source: FCs, which first encapsulate region 2b germline cysts and are defined by continued association with a single cyst, derive directly from the posterior ('layer 1') FSCs, whereas ECs derive directly from anterior FSCs in layers 2 or 3 (Reilein et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: ECs derive directly from anterior FSCs in layers 2 or 3.
source: FCs, which first encapsulate region 2b germline cysts and are defined by continued association with a single cyst, derive directly from the posterior ('layer 1') FSCs, whereas ECs derive directly from anterior FSCs in layers 2 or 3 (Reilein et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: Posterior FSCs divide faster than anterior FSCs.
source: Posterior FSCs divide faster than anterior FSCs, so that the roughly four-fold greater efflux of derivatives from the posterior face of the FSC domain is supported without significant net flow of FSCs from anterior to posterior locations (Reilein et al., 2017; Reilein et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Hedgehog (Hh) is produced in Terminal Filament and Cap cells.
source: Hh is produced in Terminal Filament and Cap cells, the anteriormost cells of the germarium, and its release is regulated by the Hedgehog binding protein Boi (Forbes et al., 1996a; Hartman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Hh promotes FSC survival and amplification principally by regulating the rate of FSC division through transcriptional induction of Yorkie (Yki).
source: Hh was shown to promote FSC survival and amplification principally by regulating the rate of FSC division through transcriptional induction of the Hippo-pathway transcriptional co-activator Yorkie (Yki) (Huang and Kalderon, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: The Wg and Wnt6 ligands are produced in Cap Cells at the anterior of the germarium.
source: The Wg and Wnt6 ligands are produced in Cap Cells at the anterior of the germarium and are supplemented by the production of Wnt2 and Wnt4 in ECs (Forbes et al., 1996b; Luo et al., 2015; Sahai-Hernandez and Nystul, 2013; Waghmare et al., 2018; Wang and Page-McCaw, 2018)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Wnt2 and Wnt4 are produced in ECs.
source: The Wg and Wnt6 ligands are produced in Cap Cells at the anterior of the germarium and are supplemented by the production of Wnt2 and Wnt4 in ECs (Forbes et al., 1996b; Luo et al., 2015; Sahai-Hernandez and Nystul, 2013; Waghmare et al., 2018; Wang and Page-McCaw, 2018)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Wnt signaling produces high levels of pathway activity over the EC domain with a sharp decline over the FSC domain and little or no activity in FCs.
source: to produce high levels of pathway activity over the EC domain with a sharp decline over the FSC domain and little or no activity in FCs (Figure 1A; Reilein et al., 2017; Wang and Page-McCaw, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: FSCs were lost from the niche cell autonomously when Wnt signaling was either genetically elevated or reduced.
source: FSCs were lost from the niche cell autonomously when Wnt signaling was either genetically elevated or reduced (Song and Xie, 2003; Vied et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Increased Wnt pathway activity favors more anterior locations and EC production, while reducing FC production.
source: More recently it was shown that the primary effects of altering Wnt pathway activity were exerted on the AP location of FSCs and their conversion to differentiated products, with increased pathway activity favoring more anterior locations and EC production, while reducing FC production (Reilein et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: Rapid loss of FSCs due to elevated Wnt pathway activity results from conversion of all FSCs over time to ECs.
source: Thus, relatively rapid loss of FSCs due to elevated Wnt pathway activity results from conversion of all FSCs over time to ECs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference from prior work.

claim: The JAK-STAT ligand Unpaired (Upd) is produced in specialized FCs called polar cells.
source: The JAK-STAT ligand Unpaired (Upd) is produced in specialized FCs called polar cells that are found at the anterior and posterior ends of developing egg chambers (Figure 1A,D; McGregor et al., 2002; Vied et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations and reference to Figure 1.

claim: JAK-STAT pathway activity is high in FCs in the germarium and decreases from posterior to anterior over the FSC domain with only low levels in ECs.
source: Pathway activity is high in FCs in the germarium and decreases from posterior to anterior over the FSC domain with only low levels in ECs (Figure 1A; Vied et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: When JAK-STAT activity was elevated in FSC lineages, these FSCs out-competed wild-type FSCs.
source: When JAK-STAT activity was elevated in FSC lineages, it was shown that these FSCs out-competed wild-type FSCs and that proliferating FSC derivatives could accumulate in EC territory.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing prior work.

claim: Loss of STAT activity resulted in accelerated FSC loss.
source: Conversely, loss of STAT activity resulted in accelerated FSC loss (Vied et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: In control clones 6d after induction, the average percentage of all GFP-marked FSCs that incorporated EdU was 25.1%.
source: In control clones 6d after induction, the average percentage of all GFP-marked FSCs that incorporated EdU was 25.1% (n = 4753) with a pronounced gradient of labeling, declining from posterior to anterior (33.4% for layer 1, 20.0% for layer 2, and 8.2% for layer 3) (Figure 2A)
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: EdU incorporation in control FSCs shows a pronounced gradient of labeling, declining from posterior to anterior (33.4% for layer 1, 20.0% for layer 2, and 8.2% for layer 3).
source: In control clones 6d after induction, the average percentage of all GFP-marked FSCs that incorporated EdU was 25.1% (n = 4753) with a pronounced gradient of labeling, declining from posterior to anterior (33.4% for layer 1, 20.0% for layer 2, and 8.2% for layer 3) (Figure 2A)
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: Only 2.4% of FSCs with homozygous null stat alleles incorporated EdU, a ten-fold reduction compared to controls.
source: We found that only 2.4% of FSCs with either of two homozygous null stat alleles incorporated EdU (n = 336), a ten-fold reduction compared to controls (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2.

claim: 43.9% of UAS-Hop FSCs incorporated EdU, nearly double the rate of control FSC clones.
source: we expressed excess levels of the only Drosophila Janus Kinase, Hopscotch (Hop) using a UAS-Hop transgene in FSC clones (Vied et al., 2012; Xi et al., 2003), and found that 43.9% of UAS-Hop FSCs incorporated EdU (n = 1379), nearly double the rate of control FSC clones (Figure 2A,C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with references to figures.

claim: The pattern of EdU incorporation in UAS-Hop FSCs still showed a posterior bias, with 49.9% of layer 1, 39.8% of layer 2, and 32.1% of layer 3 FSCs labeled by EdU.
source: The pattern of EdU incorporation in these FSCs still showed a posterior bias, with 49.9% of layer 1, 39.8% of layer 2, and 32.1% of layer 3 UAS-Hop FSCs labeled by EdU, although the EdU indices of layer 1 and layer 3 FSCs relative to the whole FSC population were significantly different from controls (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: The JAK-STAT pathway has a very strong positive, dose-responsive, cell autonomous influence on the FSC cell cycle.
source: These experiments demonstrated that the JAK-STAT pathway has a very strong positive, dose-responsive, cell autonomous influence on the FSC cell cycle.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the EdU incorporation data.

claim: After 3d at 29C with C587>Hop expression, STAT-GFP fluorescence was similar in each of the three FSC layers and also over more anterior regions.
source: After 3d at the restrictive temperature of 29C, we measured STAT-GFP fluorescence and found it to be similar in each of the three FSC layers and also over more anterior regions, indicating that the entire FSC domain now has roughly even JAK-STAT pathway activity (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is a result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2E,F.

claim: With roughly even JAK-STAT activity across the FSC region using C587>Hop, nearly identical frequencies of EdU labeling were observed in each FSC layer: 38.2% of layer 1, 37.4% of layer 2, and 41.1% of layer 3 FSCs.
source: With roughly even JAK-STAT activity across the FSC region, we measured proliferation in the three FSC layers. We observed nearly identical frequencies of EdU labeling in each FSC layer of C587>Hop germaria; 38.2% of layer 1, 37.4% of layer 2, and 41.1% of layer 3 FSCs (Figure 2G,H,J).
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2.

claim: Synthetically making JAK-STAT pathway activity uniform, rather than graded, eliminated the normal posterior to anterior gradient of EdU labeling.
source: Thus, synthetically making JAK-STAT pathway activity uniform, rather than graded, eliminated the normal posterior to anterior gradient of EdU labeling.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the C587>Hop experiment.

claim: Elevated JAK-STAT activity in the anterior of the germarium stimulated EdU incorporation in 10.4% of ECs.
source: Additionally, elevated JAK-STAT activity in the anterior of the germarium stimulated EdU incorporation in 10.4% of ECs (Figure 2H,J).
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2.

claim: Excess JAK-STAT pathway activity can suffice to initiate cell division in the EC domain.
source: Clearly, excess JAK-STAT pathway activity can suffice to initiate cell division in the EC domain, whether the target cells were recently derived from FSCs or not.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on EdU incorporation in ECs.

claim: When UAS-CycE was expressed with the C587-GAL4 driver, the profile of EdU incorporation for FSCs remained graded with a posterior bias.
source: When UAS-CycE was expressed with the C587-GAL4 driver (C587>CycE) we found that the profile of EdU incorporation for FSCs remained graded with a posterior basis, contrasting with the response to UAS-Hop, although the gradient was flatter than in control FSCs, as revealed by statistically significant differences in the relative EdU index for layer one and for layer three relative to the overall EdU index (Figure 2I,J).
evidence: This is a result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2.

claim: ECs remained quiescent when UAS-CycE was expressed with C587-GAL4.
source: Also, ECs remained quiescent.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the C587>CycE experiment.

claim: Graded JAK-STAT pathway activity instructs graded proliferation within the FSC domain.
source: We conclude that graded JAK-STAT pathway activity instructs graded proliferation within the FSC domain, and that the anterior range of sufficient JAK-STAT pathway activity appears to define the anterior boundary of this critical stem cell property.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on multiple experiments.

claim: The anterior range of sufficient JAK-STAT pathway activity appears to define the anterior boundary of FSC proliferation.
source: We conclude that graded JAK-STAT pathway activity instructs graded proliferation within the FSC domain, and that the anterior range of sufficient JAK-STAT pathway activity appears to define the anterior boundary of this critical stem cell property.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section.

claim: EdU incorporation in stat FSC clones was graded: 6.5% of marked layer 1 FSCs incorporated EdU, compared to 1.5% for layer 2 and 0% for layer 3.
source: Though EdU incorporation was very low in stat FSC clones, it was graded; 6.5% of marked layer 1 FSCs incorporated EdU, compared to 1.5% for layer 2 and 0% for layer 3 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: There appear to be other influences besides JAK-STAT that pattern FSC proliferation.
source: Thus, there appear to be other influences that pattern FSC proliferation.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the graded EdU incorporation in stat mutants.

claim: Expression of excess CycE and inactivation of Kibra and Warts do not alter the normal graded pattern of proliferation.
source: We found that expression of excess CycE and inactivation of upstream components of the Hippo/Yorkie pathway, Kibra and Warts (Wts), previously shown to influence FSC proliferation (Huang and Kalderon, 2014), appear to fulfill this requirement because the gradient of EdU labeling was largely unaltered (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2K and a citation.

claim: In the absence of graded JAK-STAT pathway activity in the marked cells, there remains a robust mechanism for imposing graded FSC proliferation.
source: In all of these experiments, more FSCs in layer one incorporated EdU compared to the anterior layers in a pattern resembling that of normal FSCs (Figure 2K). Moreover, there were no statistically significant differences from controls in the relative EdU index of any one layer relative to the whole FSC population for these genotypes (Figure 2K) or stat alone (Figure 2A), indicating that, in the absence of graded JAK-STAT pathway activity in the marked cells, there remains a robust mechanism for imposing graded FSC proliferation.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on data in Figure 2.

claim: 96.5% of stat FSCs were found in the anterior layers of the germarium by 12d.
source: When scoring germaria with stat mutant clones, we observed that 96.5% of stat FSCs were found in the anterior layers of the germarium by 12d (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: The proportion of FSCs in layer one was reduced from a control value of 48.8% to 41.0% for cycEWX hypomorphs and 43.3% for cutlet FSCs.
source: When we tested other mutants that had severely impaired proliferation, including cycE and cutlet (Wang et al., 2012; Wang and Kalderon, 2009), we observed an altered distribution of FSCs with the proportion of FSCs in layer one reduced from a control value of 48.8% to 41.0% for cycEWX hypomorphs and 43.3% for cutlet FSCs but those changes were not statistically significant and were much smaller than observed for stat mutant FSCs (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with references to citations and Figure 3A.

claim: There is a consistent anterior bias for all FSCs lacking STAT activity, even for genotypes that permitted EdU incorporation at frequencies approaching normal values.
source: Thus, we observed a consistent anterior bias for all FSCs lacking STAT activity, even for genotypes that permitted EdU incorporation at frequencies approaching normal values.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on FSC location data.

claim: A layer 1 FSC has, on average, a 61.6% likelihood of becoming an FC in one cycle for control FSCs.
source: From 556 control germaria, across 31 MARCM experiments, we found that a layer 1 FSC has, on average, a 61.6% likelihood (p=0.616) of becoming an FC in one cycle (see Materials and methods) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: A stat mutant layer 1 FSC was much less likely than controls (34.2% compared to 61.6%) to produce an FC.
source: Using this method, we found that a stat mutant layer 1 FSC was much less likely than controls (34.2% compared to 61.6%) to produce an FC (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: The average likelihood of an FSC becoming an FC was 25.3% for kibra stat, wts stat, and UAS-CycE stat genotypes (aggregated), and 22.8% for kibra UAS-CycE stat mutant FSCs.
source: The average likelihood of an FSC becoming an FC was 25.3% for these three genotypes (aggregated), and it was 22.8% for kibra UAS-CycE stat mutant FSCs (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3.

claim: FC production from layer 1 FSCs is greatly impaired in the absence of STAT activity and this reduction is not related to changes in the rate of FSC division.
source: These experiments demonstrated that FC production from its immediate precursor, a layer 1 FSC, is greatly impaired in the absence of STAT activity and that this reduction is not related to changes in the rate of FSC division.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the immediate FC method data.

claim: The probability of a layer 1 FSC becoming an FC increased from 61.6% to 78.1% for FSCs expressing UAS-Hop.
source: We also examined the consequences of increasing JAK-STAT pathway activity in a layer 1 FSC. We found that the probability of becoming an FC increased from 61.6% to 78.1% for FSCs expressing UAS-Hop (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: Layer 1 FSCs expressing both UAS-Hop and UAS-Dap had a higher probability than controls of becoming FCs (76.7% vs 61.6%).
source: Layer 1 FSCs expressing both UAS-Hop and UAS-Dap also had a higher probability than controls of becoming FCs (76.7% vs 61.6%) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: Both increased and decreased JAK-STAT pathway activity significantly affected the production of FCs from FSCs independent of FSC division rate.
source: Thus, both increased and decreased JAK-STAT pathway activity significantly affected the production of FCs from FSCs independent of FSC division rate, suggesting that the magnitude of pathway activity is an important factor in regulating this transition.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the immediate FC method data.

claim: 66% of germaria with UAS-Hop MARCM clones showed ectopic Fas3 expression at 12d after clone induction.
source: We confirmed these observations for UAS-Hop MARCM clones, finding that 66% of germaria with labeled cells in the anterior half of the germarium (the FSC and EC domains) showed ectopic Fas3 expression at 12d after clone induction (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3F.

claim: 53% of germaria included some cells with ectopic Fas3 expression by 3d when UAS-Hop was conditionally expressed using C587-GAL4, increasing to 72% by 6d and 94% by 10d.
source: Similar structures were observed in germaria where UAS-Hop was conditionally expressed using C587-GAL4 (Figure 3G). Here, 53% of germaria included some cells with ectopic Fas3 expression by 3d, increasing to 72% by 6d and 94% by 10d.
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3G.

claim: High JAK-STAT pathway alone can instruct at least some aspects of the FC phenotype even in locations where FCs do not normally form.
source: Thus, high JAK-STAT pathway alone can instruct at least some aspects of the FC phenotype even in locations where FCs do not normally form.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on ectopic Fas3 expression data.

claim: Increased Fas3 expression can partially restore FC production in the absence of JAK-STAT pathway activity.
source: To test whether Fas3 might be an important intermediate in the normal influence of JAK-STAT signaling on FC production we expressed excess Fas3 in kibra UAS-CycE stat mutant FSCs. We observed a doubling in layer 1 FSC to FC conversion (from 22.8% to 45.4%) (Figure 3C), suggesting that increased Fas3 expression can partially restore FC production in the absence of JAK-STAT pathway activity.
evidence: This is a result and conclusion stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: By 12d, there were an average of 10.4 UAS-Hop FSCs per germarium, significantly greater than the 3.3 FSCs per germarium observed in controls.
source: Accordingly, by 12d, there were an average of 10.4 UAS-Hop FSCs per germarium (counting all ovarioles), significantly greater than the 3.3 FSCs per germarium observed in controls (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3H.

claim: The proportion of ovarioles containing a marked FSC was increased with UAS-Hop expression to 75.2% compared to 62.1% in controls.
source: The proportion of ovarioles containing a marked FSC was also increased with UAS-Hop expression to 75.2% compared to 62.1% in controls (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3H.

claim: FSC clones expressing UAS-CycE had an average of 5.6 marked FSCs per ovariole by 12d and 64.3% of ovarioles containing a marked FSC.
source: However, the increase was more modest for CycE overexpression, with an average of 5.6 marked FSCs per ovariole by 12d and 64.3% of ovarioles containing a marked FSC (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3H.

claim: When STAT activity was eliminated in FSC clones, there was an average of 0.3 stat FSCs per germarium and 25.3% of germaria retained a marked FSC after 12d.
source: When STAT activity was eliminated in FSC clones, there was an average of 0.3 stat FSCs per germarium and 25.3% of germaria retained a marked FSC after 12d (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3H.

claim: For kibra stat, wts stat, and UAS-CycE stat genotypes, the average number of FSCs increased to 2.1 per germarium with 68.5% of germaria containing an FSC clone.
source: When we tested kibra stat, wts stat, and UAS-CycE stat genotypes, the average number of FSCs increased to 2.1 per germarium with 68.5% of germaria containing an FSC clone.
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section.

claim: For kibra stat mutants expressing UAS-CycE, the average number of marked FSCs was 15.9 per germarium and 94% of ovarioles included marked FSCs.
source: This disparity was even more pronounced when examining FSC competition for kibra stat mutants expressing UAS-CycE, which had an average EdU index about 64% of wild-type. Here, the average number of marked FSCs was extremely high at 15.9 per germarium and 94% of ovarioles included marked FSCs (Figure 3E,H).
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3.

claim: The dramatically increased competitive success of FSCs lacking STAT activity for a given division rate very likely results from reduced conversion to FCs.
source: The remarkable persistence and amplification of these FSCs shows that factors other than division rate are also major determinants of FSC competition. Specifically, the dramatically increased competitive success of FSCs lacking STAT activity for a given division rate very likely results from reduced conversion to FCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on FSC competition data.

claim: 77.6% of arr FSCs but only 15–20% of axn and apc FSCs were observed in layer 1.
source: FSCs with a null arrow (arr) mutation to eliminate the Wnt pathway response and axin (axn) or Adenomatous Polyposis Coli (apc) mutations to constitutively activate the Wnt pathway in MARCM clones (Reilein et al., 2017), all illustrated a strong effect of higher Wnt signaling activity favoring anterior FSC locations and greater conversion to ECs; 77.6% of arr FSCs but only 15–20% of axn and apc FSCs were observed in layer 1
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with a citation.

claim: 9.1 axn and apc ECs and 0.1 arr ECs were observed per germarium, compared to an average of 1.5 ECs for controls.
source: while 9.1 axn and apc ECs and 0.1 arr ECs were observed per germarium, compared to an average of 1.5 ECs for controls (Reilein et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with a citation.

claim: 63.0% of UAS-dnTCF FSCs were observed in layer 1 (compared to 48.8% for controls).
source: Here we also tested the effect of reducing rather than eliminating Wnt pathway activity by expression of a UAS-dnTCF transgene (van de Wetering et al., 2002) in clones. We found that 63.0% of UAS-dnTCF FSCs were observed in layer 1 (compared to 48.8% for controls), a significant change but less pronounced than for arr FSCs, which showed a layer 1 occupancy of 79.3% across three replicates (n = 237 cells), including two additional tests not previously reported (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with references to a citation and Figure 4A.

claim: arr layer 1 FSC clones had a significantly elevated probability (76.9% compared to 61.6% in controls) of becoming an FC.
source: We also used the 'immediate FC' method to measure FC production. We found that arr layer 1 FSC clones had a significantly elevated probability (76.9% compared to 61.6% in controls) of becoming an FC, (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: Reducing Wnt pathway activity with UAS-dnTCF did not increase conversion of layer 1 FSCs to FCs (52.9% probability).
source: By contrast, reducing Wnt pathway activity with UAS-dnTCF did not increase conversion of layer 1 FSCs to FCs (52.9% probability).
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section.

claim: FSCs with increased Wnt activity showed only a 22.4% likelihood of becoming an FC, a roughly threefold decrease from control values.
source: We also observed that FSCs with increased Wnt activity showed only a 22.4% likelihood of becoming an FC, a roughly threefold decrease from control values (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: The EC/aFSC ratio was 0.55 for the period from 0-6d and 0.63 for the period from 0-12d in controls.
source: In controls, we found that the EC/aFSC ratio was 0.55 (SE 0.30; SEM 0.01) for the period from 0-6d and 0.63 (SE 0.33; SEM 0.01) for the period from 0-12d (Figure 4D; median and other statistical measures are in Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 4.

claim: Marked ECs must be lost at a significant frequency.
source: If ECs were produced by FSCs at a constant rate and all labeled ECs accumulated without loss, we would expect the 0-12d ratio to be double the 0-6d ratio. The observed percentage increase was much lower (15%) across 31 control tests, suggesting that marked ECs must also be lost at a significant frequency.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on EC/aFSC ratio data.

claim: The relatively high turnover inferred for marked ECs must apply only to ECs newly-produced from FSCs and not to the bulk EC population present at the time of adult eclosion.
source: Clearly, if this rate of EC loss applied to the whole population of over 30 ECs, far outnumbering the total of about eight anterior FSCs, there would be a severe net loss of ECs over time. We therefore deduce that the relatively high turnover that we infer for marked ECs must apply only to ECs newly-produced from FSCs and not to the bulk EC population present at the time of adult eclosion.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on EC turnover analysis.

claim: EC production was drastically reduced for arr mutant FSCs at 12d (0.11 ECs per anterior FSC compared to 0.63 for controls) and less severely at 6d (0.30 vs 0.55).
source: We found that EC production was drastically reduced for arr mutant FSCs at 12d (0.11 ECs per anterior FSC compared to 0.63 for controls) and less severely at 6d (0.30 vs 0.55) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 4D.

claim: In FSCs expressing UAS-dnTCF there was a severe loss of marked ECs at 12d relative to controls (0.22 vs 0.63) but not at 6d.
source: Similarly, in FSCs expressing UAS-dnTCF there was a severe loss of marked ECs at 12d relative to controls (0.22 vs 0.63) but not at 6d (Figure 4D)
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 4D.

claim: Reduction and especially loss of Wnt signaling greatly reduced the net conversion of marked anterior FSCs to ECs.
source: These data indicated that reduction, and especially loss of Wnt signaling greatly reduced the net conversion of marked anterior FSCs to ECs. This may be due to reduced conversion of anterior FSCs to ECs, increased turnover of ECs derived from FSCs, or both.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on EC production data.

claim: Loss of Wnt pathway activity is known to elicit apoptosis in ECs.
source: Loss of Wnt pathway activity is known to elicit apoptosis in ECs (Wang et al., 2015; Wang and Page-McCaw, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations.

claim: When UAS-DIAP1 was expressed in arr mutant FSCs, EC accumulation was increased relative to arr alone at both 6d (0.39 vs 0.30) and 12d (0.21 vs 0.11, p=0.06) but remained much below control values.
source: We found that when we expressed UAS-DIAP1 in arr mutant FSCs, EC accumulation was increased relative to arr alone at both 6d (0.39 vs 0.30) and 12d (0.21 vs 0.11, p=0.06) but remained much below control values (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 4D.

claim: When Wnt pathway activity was increased using the axn and apc mutations, the average ratio of ECs per anterior FSC was 2.0 from 0-6d and 7.3 from 0-12d.
source: When Wnt pathway activity was increased using the axn and apc mutations we found the average ratio of ECs per anterior FSC to be 2.0 from 0-6d and 7.3 from 0-12d, revealing a greatly elevated rate of EC accumulation (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 4D.

claim: When STAT activity was eliminated, EC production increased to 0.88 ECs per anterior FSC from 0-6d and 1.2 ECs per anterior FSC from 0-12d.
source: We also investigated JAK-STAT signaling and EC production dynamics. When STAT activity was eliminated, we found that EC production increased to 0.88 ECs per anterior FSC from 0-6d and 1.2 ECs per anterior FSC from 0-12d (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: EdU incorporation was slightly reduced in all layers for FSCs lacking arr activity (26.3%, 15.3%, 4.0% for layers 1–3) or expressing dnTCF (24.9%, 15.2%, 5.4% for layers 1–3) relative to controls (33.4%, 20.0%, 8.2% for layers 1–3).
source: We found that EdU incorporation was slightly reduced in all layers for FSCs lacking arr activity (26.3%, 15.3%, 4.0% for layers 1–3) or expressing dnTCF (24.9%, 15.2%, 5.4% for layers 1–3) relative to controls (33.4%, 20.0%, 8.2% for layers 1–3); the differences in layer one were statistically significant (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 4E.

claim: In response to increased Wnt pathway activity, the EdU index was substantially reduced in all layers (13.7%, 4.8%, 2.8% for layers 1–3) but a posterior to anterior gradient was still evident.
source: In response to increased Wnt pathway activity, the EdU index was substantially reduced in all layers (13.7%, 4.8%, 2.8% for layers 1–3) but a posterior to anterior gradient was still evident (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 4E.

claim: Graded FSC proliferation does not rely on graded Wnt signaling.
source: This result is consistent with the evidence from MARCM clones that graded FSC proliferation does not rely on graded Wnt signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on C587>dnTCF experiment.

claim: Neither decreased nor increased JAK-STAT pathway activity significantly altered Fz3-RFP expression.
source: Neither decreased (stat and kibra UAS-CycE stat) nor increased (UAS-Hop) JAK-STAT pathway activity significantly altered Fz3-RFP expression, suggesting no direct, cell autonomous effect of JAK-STAT signaling on Wnt signal transduction (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is a result stated in the Results section with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: Neither FSCs expressing UAS-dnTCF nor those with axn mutations had significantly altered STAT-RFP expression.
source: Neither FSCs expressing UAS-dnTCF nor those with axn mutations (together with UAS-CycE in order to increase FSC numbers) had significantly altered STAT-RFP expression suggesting that the magnitude of Wnt pathway activity does not cell autonomously affect JAK-STAT pathway signal transduction (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is a result stated in the Results section with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: Expressing UAS-dnTCF increased EdU incorporation in FSCs lacking STAT activity (from 2.4% to 4.5%).
source: It was therefore surprising that expressing UAS-dnTCF increased EdU incorporation in FSCs lacking STAT activity (from 2.4% to 4.5%).
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section.

claim: A five-fold reduction of EdU incorporation (5% vs 25%) due to the stat kibra/wts/UAS-CycE genotype was largely suppressed when Wnt pathway was reduced by UAS-dnTCF.
source: This effect was more striking in STAT-deficient genotypes with higher division rates, elevating the EdU index of FSCs with stat mutations together with kibra, wts, or UAS-CycE from an average of 4.9% to 16.2% (Figure 5A), close to the value observed for otherwise normal FSCs expressing dn-TCF (19.0%). In other words, a five-fold reduction of EdU incorporation (5% vs 25%) due to the stat kibra/wts/UAS-CycE genotype was largely suppressed when Wnt pathway was reduced by UAS-dnTCF.
evidence: This is a result and conclusion stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: The increased FSC division induced by increased JAK-STAT pathway activity (43.9% EdU index) was not significantly altered by addition of dnTCF (46.3%) and was only slightly reduced by loss of arr function (37.7%).
source: By contrast, the increased FSC division induced by increased JAK-STAT pathway activity (43.9% EdU index) was not significantly altered by addition of dnTCF (46.3%) and was only slightly reduced by loss of arr function (37.7%) (Figure 5B; Figure 5—figure supplement 3A; Figure 6).
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with references to figures.

claim: Inhibitory actions of the Wnt pathway can be strong and dose-dependent but are strongly suppressed by JAK-STAT pathway activity under conditions when both pathways are unaltered or both are artificially elevated.
source: Thus, inhibitory actions of the Wnt pathway can be strong and dose-dependent but are strongly suppressed by JAK-STAT pathway activity under conditions when both pathways are unaltered or both are artificially elevated.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on EdU incorporation data.

claim: Increased JAK-STAT activity favored conversion of layer 1 FSCs to FCs (78.1% probability) and this was further increased by loss of arr activity (90.3% for arr UAS-Hop FSCs) to a level higher than induced by Wnt signaling deficiency alone (76.9% for arr FSCs).
source: Increased JAK-STAT activity favored conversion of layer 1 FSCs to FCs (78.1% probability) and this was further increased by loss of arr activity (90.3% for arr UAS-Hop FSCs) to a level higher than induced by Wnt signaling deficiency alone (76.9% for arr FSCs) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 6A.

claim: The combination of eliminating the normally low levels of Wnt signaling and increasing the already high levels of JAK-STAT pathway in layer 1 FSCs potently accelerated and almost mandated conversion of layer 1 FSCs to FCs.
source: Thus, the combination of eliminating the normally low levels of Wnt signaling and increasing the already high levels of JAK-STAT pathway in layer 1 FSCs potently accelerated and almost mandated conversion of layer 1 FSCs to FCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on FC production data.

claim: 87.1% of arr UAS-Hop FSCs were found in layer 1, representing an enhancement of the bias seen for arr FSCs (79.3%).
source: Moreover, despite accelerated loss from layer one to become FCs, 87.1% of arr UAS-Hop FSCs were found in this layer, representing an enhancement of the bias seen for arr FSCs (79.3%) (Figure 6D)
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 6D.

claim: High JAK-STAT activity overcame the normally strong inhibition of FC production by elevated Wnt pathway activity.
source: High JAK-STAT activity also overcame the normally strong inhibition of FC production by elevated Wnt pathway activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on FC production data.

claim: The average number of marked cells in the EC region per germarium at 12d was 1.3 for controls and 3.3 for UAS-Hop lineages, was greatly reduced for arr UAS-Hop (0.07), reduced to a lesser degree for UAS-dnTCF UAS-Hop, and greatly increased for axn UAS-Hop (17.2) FSC lineages.
source: The average number of marked cells in the EC region per germarium at 12d, which was 1.3 for controls and 3.3 for UAS-Hop lineages, was greatly reduced for arr UAS-Hop (0.07), reduced to a lesser degree for UAS-dnTCF UAS-Hop, and greatly increased for axn UAS-Hop (17.2) FSC lineages (Figure 6E,G–I)
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 6.

claim: EC production is still highly responsive to changes in Wnt pathway activity in both directions even when JAK-STAT pathway activity is elevated.
source: showing that EC production is still highly responsive to changes in Wnt pathway activity in both directions even when JAK-STAT pathway activity is elevated.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on EC production data.

claim: Epistasis tests reveal a primary role of Wnt signaling for differentiation decisions in anterior regions and a primary role for JAK-STAT signaling for differentiation decisions in posterior regions.
source: Thus, epistasis tests reveal a primary role of Wnt signaling for differentiation decisions in anterior regions and a primary role for JAK-STAT signaling for differentiation decisions in posterior regions.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on epistasis experiments.

claim: Elevated JAK-STAT activity increased the average FSC number to 10.4 per germarium, largely by increasing division rates.
source: Elevated JAK-STAT activity increased the average FSC number to 10.4 per germarium, largely by increasing division rates (Figure 6J).
evidence: This is a result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 6J.

claim: Complete Wnt pathway inhibition with arr UAS-Hop drastically reduced the 12d average FSC population to 0.3 per germarium, with only 17.8% of ovarioles retaining any marked FSCs.
source: However, complete Wnt pathway inhibition greatly increased FSC concentration in layer 1 (Figure 6D) and enhanced conversion from layer one to FCs (Figure 6A,F), with the net effect of drastically reducing the 12d average FSC population to 0.3 per germarium, with only 17.8% of ovarioles retaining any marked FSCs (Figure 6G,J).
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with references to figures.

claim: Even a greatly elevated FSC division rate cannot maintain a sufficient supply of marked FSCs when they are drained by posterior flux and conversion to FCs at the high rates promoted by a combination of high JAK-STAT pathway activity and elimination of Wnt pathway activity.
source: Thus, even a greatly elevated FSC division rate cannot maintain a sufficient supply of marked FSCs when they are drained by posterior flux and conversion to FCs at the high rates promoted by a combination of high JAK-STAT pathway activity and elimination of Wnt pathway activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on FSC competition data.

claim: With elevated Wnt signaling in axn UAS-Hop mutant lineages, labeled FSCs accumulated to 28.1 FSCs per germarium, exceeding the normal capacity of the germarium.
source: Accordingly, labeled FSCs accumulated to an even greater extent than for UAS-Hop alone and indeed exceeded the normal capacity of the germarium at 28.1 axn UAS-Hop FSCs per germarium (Figure 6H–J).
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 6.

claim: Changes in Wnt pathway activity profoundly altered the competitive success of FSCs with elevated JAK-STAT pathway activity by either promoting (loss of Wnt) or reducing (elevated Wnt) FC production, without significantly altering FSC division rates in either case.
source: Thus, changes in Wnt pathway activity profoundly altered the competitive success of FSCs with elevated JAK-STAT pathway activity by either promoting (loss of Wnt) or reducing (elevated Wnt) FC production, without significantly altering FSC division rates in either case.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on FSC competition data.

claim: JAK-STAT pathway activity is the primary dose-dependent agent dictating the pattern of FSC proliferation.
source: The results reveal JAK-STAT pathway activity as the primary dose-dependent agent dictating the pattern of FSC proliferation and as a major influence promoting conversion of FSCs to FCs.
evidence: This is a main conclusion stated in the Discussion.

claim: JAK-STAT pathway activity is a major influence promoting conversion of FSCs to FCs.
source: The results reveal JAK-STAT pathway activity as the primary dose-dependent agent dictating the pattern of FSC proliferation and as a major influence promoting conversion of FSCs to FCs.
evidence: This is a main conclusion stated in the Discussion.

claim: Wnt pathway magnitude relative to neighboring FSCs is a major determinant of the AP position of an FSC and its conversion to an EC.
source: Wnt pathway magnitude relative to neighboring FSCs was previously shown to be a major determinant of the AP position of an FSC and its conversion to an EC (Reilein et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation.

claim: Elevated Wnt pathway activity inhibits FC production.
source: Here we found that elevated Wnt pathway activity also inhibits FC production while elimination of Wnt pathway activity promotes conversion of posterior FSCs to FCs.
evidence: This is a main finding stated in the Discussion.

claim: Elimination of Wnt pathway activity promotes conversion of posterior FSCs to FCs.
source: Here we found that elevated Wnt pathway activity also inhibits FC production while elimination of Wnt pathway activity promotes conversion of posterior FSCs to FCs.
evidence: This is a main finding stated in the Discussion.

claim: The graded nature of both JAK-STAT and Wnt pathways plays a crucial role in determining the A/P extent of the FSC domain and, consequently, the number of FSCs supported.
source: Thus, the graded nature of both pathways plays a crucial role in determining the A/P extent of the FSC domain and, consequently, the number of FSCs supported.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion.
